overview: dbt Documentation is the practice of attaching human-readable descriptions to models, columns, sources, and other resources - written in schema YAML files and reusable doc blocks - so that a project's meaning travels with its code and can be published as a searchable website.

dbt Lineage is the automatically-derived directed acyclic graph (DAG) of dependencies between models and sources, built entirely from the ref() and source() functions in your SQL; it powers impact analysis, debugging, and onboarding without anyone hand-drawing a diagram.

Both features are produced by `dbt docs generate`, which compiles the project into two artifacts - manifest.json (the graph, configs, and descriptions) and catalog.json (column types and stats read from the warehouse information schema) - that a static docs site then renders with an interactive lineage graph.
learningObjectives: Write model and column descriptions in schema.yml, and factor long descriptions into reusable {% docs %} blocks referenced with the doc() function.
Explain how ref() and source() create edges in the DAG, and how dbt builds the lineage graph and the manifest.json artifact from them.

Generate and serve the documentation site, use lineage for impact analysis, and apply exposures, groups/access, meta/tags, and persist_docs to govern and surface a real staging -> intermediate -> marts project.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: dbt documentation is a set of descriptive metadata (descriptions, meta, tags) declared in YAML schema files and Markdown doc blocks, associated with resources (models, sources, seeds, snapshots, macros, exposures) in the project. Lineage is the dependency graph dbt constructs by statically parsing ref() and source() calls to form a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are resources and whose edges are 'depends-on' relationships. `dbt docs generate` compiles the project and warehouse metadata into two JSON artifacts: manifest.json (a full description of every node, its config, description, and dependency edges) and catalog.json (per-relation column names, data types, and statistics queried from the database's information schema). `dbt docs serve` renders these artifacts as a browsable website featuring per-model documentation and an interactive DAG.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of your dbt project as a city of data tables. Every model is a building, and ref() is the road that connects one building to another. dbt walks all those roads and automatically draws you a map (the lineage graph) - you never have to draw it yourself, and it is always up to date. Documentation is the plaque you put on each building and each room (model and column descriptions) explaining what it is for. `dbt docs generate` takes photos of the whole city and its plaques and prints a guidebook (a website) so a new teammate can find their way around, and so that when one building needs repairs you can instantly see which roads - and which downstream dashboards - are affected.
coreConcept.historicalContext: dbt (data build tool) was created by Fishtown Analytics (now dbt Labs) starting around 2016 to bring software-engineering discipline - version control, testing, and modularity - to SQL-based analytics transformation. Documentation and the auto-generated lineage graph were among its earliest differentiators: because ref() already declared dependencies for build ordering, dbt could reuse that same graph to render lineage for free. The manifest.json artifact became the backbone of many later features, including state comparison and Slim CI (dbt 0.18+, 2020). Exposures were introduced in dbt 0.18.1 to represent downstream consumers like dashboards. More recently (dbt 1.5, 2023) groups and model access modifiers - public, private, protected - added governance and contracts to larger multi-team projects, and `dbt docs generate --static` produced a single self-contained HTML file for easy hosting.

whyItMatters.business: Documented, lineage-aware data lets analysts and stakeholders trust and correctly interpret metrics, reduces repeated 'what does this column mean?' questions, and makes audits and data-governance requirements (knowing where sensitive data flows) tractable rather than a manual archaeology project.
whyItMatters.engineering: Lineage turns 'if I change this staging model, what breaks?' from guesswork into a one-click impact analysis, dramatically shortening debugging and safe-refactoring cycles; descriptions embedded in the repo keep documentation in sync with code because they live in the same pull request.
whyItMatters.scalability: As projects grow to hundreds or thousands of models across many teams, the auto-generated DAG and groups/access modifiers keep the mental model manageable, enforce which models are safe public interfaces, and let CI build only what changed using the manifest and state selection.
whyItMatters.cost: Impact analysis prevents expensive mistakes (dropping a column that feeds a revenue dashboard); state-based selection (`state:modified+`) lets CI and production runs rebuild only affected models instead of everything, cutting warehouse compute; persist_docs surfaces descriptions in the warehouse so consumers do not spin up ad-hoc discovery queries.
whyItMatters.reliability: Because lineage is derived from the same ref()/source() calls dbt uses to order the build, the documentation graph can never silently drift from execution reality; exposures make downstream dependencies explicit so a model change that would break a dashboard is visible before it ships.

coreComponents.name: Schema YAML files (schema.yml)
coreComponents.definition: YAML files (conventionally models/<folder>/schema.yml or _<folder>__models.yml) that declare resources under keys like models: and sources:, attaching a description, columns (each with its own description and tests), meta, tags, config, and access.
coreComponents.purpose: To describe what each model and column means, define data tests, and configure governance metadata in version-controlled YAML alongside the SQL.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Associate descriptions and metadata with models/columns/sources, declare tests and contracts, and provide the descriptive text that flows into manifest.json and the docs site.
coreComponents.examples:
models:
  - name: stg_orders
    description: "Cleaned one-row-per-order staging model."
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: "Primary key."

coreComponents.name: Doc blocks ({% docs %} ... {% enddocs %}) and the doc() function
coreComponents.definition: Named Markdown blocks defined in .md files inside the project using {% docs block_name %}...{% enddocs %}, referenced from YAML descriptions via the Jinja function {{ doc('block_name') }}.
coreComponents.purpose: To write rich, reusable, Markdown-formatted documentation once and reference it from many models/columns, keeping long prose out of YAML.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Store shared explanations (e.g., a standard 'order_status' enum), support Markdown formatting (tables, lists, links), and be resolved during compilation so the rendered site shows formatted text.
coreComponents.examples: In docs.md: {% docs order_status %} One of: placed, shipped, returned. {% enddocs %} | In YAML: description: \"{{ doc('order_status') }}\"

coreComponents.name: Artifacts: manifest.json and catalog.json
coreComponents.definition: manifest.json is the compiled representation of the entire project - every node, its compiled SQL, config, description, tags, and its depends_on edges; catalog.json holds per-relation column names, data types, and statistics gathered by querying the warehouse information schema.
coreComponents.purpose: To serve as the machine-readable source of truth for the docs site, the lineage graph, state comparison, and downstream tooling.
coreComponents.responsibilities: manifest.json encodes structure and lineage and drives state selection; catalog.json supplies observed column/type/stat metadata; together they render the documentation website.
coreComponents.examples: target/manifest.json (nodes + depends_on) | target/catalog.json (column types) | dbt build --select state:modified+ --state ./prod-artifacts

coreComponents.name: Lineage DAG (ref/source dependency graph)
coreComponents.definition: The directed acyclic graph whose nodes are dbt resources and whose edges come from ref() and source() calls; sources() point at raw upstream tables, ref() points at other dbt models.
coreComponents.purpose: To determine build order, enable graph-based selection (model+, +model), and render the interactive lineage visualization.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Order execution topologically, detect cycles (which are errors), power selection syntax, and back the lineage graph and impact analysis in the docs UI.
coreComponents.examples: raw.jaffle.orders (source) -> stg_orders -> int_orders_joined -> fct_orders -> exposure: 'Revenue Dashboard'

coreComponents.name: Governance metadata: exposures, groups, access, meta, tags
coreComponents.definition: exposures declare downstream consumers (dashboards, apps, ML) that depend on models; groups bundle models under an owner; access modifiers (public/private/protected) control which models may be ref()'d from outside their group; meta and tags attach arbitrary key-values and labels.
coreComponents.purpose: To extend lineage past the warehouse boundary, define ownership and safe public interfaces, and classify resources for selection and discovery.
coreComponents.responsibilities: exposures add downstream nodes to the DAG; groups+access enforce interface boundaries at parse time; meta/tags enrich the catalog and enable tag-based selection and filtering.
coreComponents.examples: exposures: - name: revenue_dashboard, type: dashboard, depends_on: [ref('fct_orders')] | access: public | tags: ['pii', 'finance']

internalWorking: Parsing phase: dbt reads every .sql and .yml file and, using Jinja, statically resolves ref() and source() calls without executing SQL. Each ref('model_x') becomes a depends_on.nodes edge and each source('src','tbl') a depends_on.sources edge, so the entire dependency graph is known from the code alone before any query runs.

Graph construction: dbt assembles these edges into a directed acyclic graph. It validates the graph is acyclic (a cycle, e.g. A refs B and B refs A, is a hard error) and computes a topological order that guarantees every upstream model is built before its dependents; this same graph backs both build ordering and the lineage visualization.

Compilation and manifest: dbt renders each model's Jinja into executable SQL (ref() becomes the fully-qualified relation name for the target environment) and writes manifest.json - a complete inventory of nodes with their compiled SQL, config, descriptions (with doc() blocks resolved to text), meta, tags, and depends_on edges. This artifact is the single source of truth for the docs site and for state comparison.

Catalog population: `dbt docs generate` additionally runs metadata queries against the warehouse's information schema (or equivalent) for each built relation, collecting column names, data types, and available statistics (row counts, bytes), and writes them to catalog.json. This is why the models must generally exist in the warehouse for the catalog to be complete; manifest.json alone reflects the code, catalog.json reflects the live database.

Serving: `dbt docs serve` starts a lightweight local web server that loads manifest.json and catalog.json and renders the documentation website - per-resource pages merging code-side descriptions with warehouse-side column types, plus an interactive DAG where clicking a node highlights all upstream (ancestors) and downstream (descendants) dependencies for instant impact analysis. `--static` instead bakes everything into one self-contained HTML file.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: source() / ref() in SQL -> parse & resolve dependencies -> build DAG (topological order) -> compile SQL + write manifest.json -> query warehouse information schema -> write catalog.json -> dbt docs serve renders website (per-model docs + interactive lineage) -> exposures extend DAG to downstream dashboards/apps
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. An engineer writes stg_orders.sql selecting from {{ source('jaffle', 'orders') }} and fct_orders.sql selecting from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}, and adds descriptions in schema.yml plus a shared {% docs %} block for the order_status enum.

2. Running `dbt docs generate` triggers parsing: dbt resolves the source() and ref() calls, recording that stg_orders depends on the jaffle.orders source and fct_orders depends on stg_orders - forming DAG edges - then compiles the SQL and writes manifest.json with those edges and the resolved descriptions.
3. dbt then queries the warehouse information schema for the built relations, capturing each column's data type and stats, and writes catalog.json.

4. `dbt docs serve` reads both artifacts and renders the site: the fct_orders page shows its description, its column types from the catalog, the order_status doc block text, and a lineage graph where clicking fct_orders highlights jaffle.orders -> stg_orders -> fct_orders upstream and the revenue_dashboard exposure downstream, giving a full picture for onboarding and impact analysis.

keyTerminology.meaning: Jinja functions that declare dependencies: ref('model') points at another dbt model, source('name','table') points at a raw upstream table. dbt substitutes them with fully-qualified relation names at compile time.
keyTerminology.importance: They are the sole source of the lineage graph and build order; using them (instead of hard-coding table names) is what makes lineage automatic and environment-portable.

keyTerminology.meaning: The compiled artifact in target/ describing every node, its config, compiled SQL, description, tags, and depends_on edges - effectively the full graph plus metadata.
keyTerminology.importance: It powers the docs site, the lineage graph, and state-based selection (state:modified+); many external tools consume it as dbt's machine-readable project representation.

keyTerminology.meaning: The artifact produced by docs generate holding per-relation column names, data types, and statistics gathered from the warehouse information schema.
keyTerminology.importance: It provides the observed database-side metadata (types/stats) the docs site shows, complementing the code-side descriptions in manifest.json.

keyTerminology.meaning: A YAML-defined node representing a downstream consumer (dashboard, application, ML model, notebook) that depends on one or more dbt models via depends_on.
keyTerminology.importance: Exposures extend lineage beyond the warehouse so you can see which BI/apps break if a model changes, closing the impact-analysis loop end to end.

keyTerminology.meaning: A per-model property (with groups) declaring whether a model may be ref()'d from outside its group: private (same group only), protected (same project), public (anyone).
keyTerminology.importance: It turns models into governed interfaces, preventing teams from depending on another team's internal implementation details.

importantConcepts.concept: How ref() creates the lineage graph (and why it is trustworthy)
importantConcepts.explanation: In dbt you never write a raw table name in a model's FROM clause; you write {{ ref('other_model') }}. During parsing, dbt records each ref() as a directed edge from the referenced model to the referencing model, and each source() as an edge from a raw table to the model. Because dbt needs this same graph to decide build order (upstream first) and to enable selection syntax like `stg_orders+` (a model and everything downstream), the lineage you see in the docs is exactly the graph dbt executes - it cannot drift from reality the way a hand-maintained diagram does. This dual use is the key insight: dependency declaration for correctness and lineage documentation are one and the same, which is why adopting ref()/source() consistently is non-negotiable. Hard-coding a table name bypasses the graph, breaking both build ordering and lineage.

importantConcepts.concept: Documentation lives in the repo: descriptions, doc blocks, and persist_docs
importantConcepts.explanation: Descriptions are declared in schema.yml at the model and column level; for long or reusable prose you define a {% docs block_name %}...{% enddocs %} block in a .md file and reference it as description: "{{ doc('block_name') }}". Because this text is versioned alongside the SQL, updating a model and its documentation happen in the same pull request and review, keeping them in sync - the classic failure mode of external wikis is that they rot. The persist_docs config (set in dbt_project.yml or a model config) pushes these descriptions into the warehouse as table and column COMMENTs, so consumers using the database directly, or downstream BI catalogs, see the same descriptions without opening the dbt docs site. This means a single source of truth - the dbt project - can surface documentation in three places: the docs website, the warehouse metadata, and any tool that reads manifest.json.

variationsAndTypes: **Description placement:** inline text in schema.yml vs. reusable {% docs %} blocks referenced with doc(); inline is quick for one-offs, doc blocks are best for shared/long/Markdown-rich content.

**Artifact scope:** manifest.json (code-derived graph + descriptions, always produced by parse/compile) vs. catalog.json (warehouse-derived column types/stats, produced by docs generate against a built database).
**Serving modes:** `dbt docs serve` (local web server reading target artifacts) vs. `dbt docs generate --static` (single self-contained HTML file for easy hosting/sharing).

**Lineage granularity:** model-level lineage (node-to-node edges from ref/source, always available) vs. column-level lineage (which upstream columns feed a column, available in dbt Cloud / Explorer and some tools, not in open-source docs by default).

**Governance metadata:** exposures (downstream consumers), groups + access modifiers (public/private/protected interfaces and ownership), and meta/tags (arbitrary metadata and labels) - each extends what the graph and docs can express.
advantages: **Always-accurate lineage:** the DAG is derived from the same ref()/source() calls dbt executes, so it never drifts from reality and requires zero manual upkeep.

**Fast impact analysis and onboarding:** clicking a node shows all upstream and downstream dependencies (including exposures), turning refactoring risk assessment and new-hire orientation into a browsing exercise.

**Documentation stays in sync:** descriptions and doc blocks live in the repo and ship in the same PR as the code, avoiding the rot of external wikis, and persist_docs mirrors them into the warehouse.
**Reusable and machine-readable:** doc() blocks let you write once and reference everywhere, while manifest.json/catalog.json expose the whole project to external tooling and state-based CI.
disadvantages: **Catalog requires a built warehouse:** column types/stats in catalog.json come from querying the database, so incomplete or unbuilt models yield gaps, and generating the catalog adds metadata queries.
**Open-source column-level lineage is limited:** node-level lineage is free, but true column-level lineage generally needs dbt Cloud/Explorer or third-party tools.
**Discipline-dependent quality:** empty descriptions and missing doc coverage produce a technically-correct but unhelpful site; documentation quality is only as good as the team's habits.

**Static site can go stale for consumers:** a hosted --static/manifest snapshot reflects the moment it was generated, so it must be regenerated in CI/CD to stay current for viewers who do not run dbt.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Always use ref()/source() and maintain descriptions - this is standard practice for any dbt project. Use doc() blocks for shared/long descriptions, exposures to capture BI/app dependencies, groups+access for multi-team projects, and persist_docs when consumers query the warehouse directly. Regenerate docs in CI/CD so the site and manifest stay current.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid hard-coding table names (never write raw FROM schema.table where a ref/source belongs) as it breaks lineage and build order. Do not rely on catalog.json for models that are not built. Do not treat a one-time locally-generated docs site as a living document - if consumers depend on it, automate regeneration. Column-level lineage in open-source is limited; reach for dbt Explorer or dedicated tools when you truly need it.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: dbt lineage is like the wiring diagram of a house that draws itself. Every time an electrician (a model) plugs into an outlet (ref/source), the diagram automatically adds the wire - nobody redraws it by hand, so it is always correct. Documentation is the label on each outlet and breaker ('kitchen lights', 'garage'), and the {% docs %} block is a shared legend you write once and reuse. `dbt docs generate` prints the whole labeled diagram into a binder (the website); exposures are the note that says 'this circuit also powers the neighbor's porch light', so before you cut power to a wire you can instantly see everything - inside the house and out - that goes dark.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You have to draw the lineage graph or keep it updated manually.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You never draw it. dbt derives the entire DAG automatically from the ref() and source() calls in your SQL. As long as you use those functions instead of hard-coded table names, the lineage is always accurate and free - regenerating docs simply re-reads the code.

commonMisconceptions.myth: `dbt docs generate` builds your models, and the catalog reflects the code.
commonMisconceptions.reality: docs generate does not run your models; it compiles them and then queries the warehouse's information schema for already-built relations to populate catalog.json. If a model has not been built (via dbt run/build), its column types and stats will be missing from the catalog even though it appears in manifest.json.

productionConsiderations.scalability: For large projects (hundreds/thousands of models), lean on groups and access modifiers to define team boundaries and public interfaces, use tags for selection, and generate docs in CI so the manifest stays current; state-based selection (state:modified+) keeps runs proportional to what changed rather than the whole graph.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Because lineage comes from the executed ref()/source() graph it cannot silently drift; enforce ref() usage in code review (and with tooling/linters like dbt-checkpoint or SQLFluff) so no model bypasses the graph via hard-coded tables.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Detect and reject dependency cycles at parse time (dbt errors on them); use exposures to make downstream breakage visible before deploy, and validate that referenced doc() blocks exist so docs generate does not fail on missing references.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track documentation coverage (percentage of models/columns with non-empty descriptions), exposure freshness, and source freshness; some teams enforce coverage in CI so undocumented models fail the build.
productionConsiderations.security: Use tags like 'pii' and meta fields to classify sensitive columns, then use lineage to trace where that data flows; access modifiers prevent unauthorized cross-team dependencies; be mindful that a publicly-hosted docs site exposes schema/column names and descriptions.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Generate the catalog only where needed (its information-schema queries add cost on very wide schemas); use state:modified+ so CI rebuilds only affected models; persist_docs lets consumers read descriptions from warehouse comments instead of running discovery queries.
productionConsiderations.performance: manifest.json parsing/compilation scales with project size; use partial parsing (default) to speed re-runs, and prefer --static or CI-generated artifacts for viewers rather than making everyone run docs generate locally.

codeExamples.title: schema.yml: model and column descriptions, exposures, meta, tags, access
codeExamples.overview: A schema file for a marts model with column descriptions and a doc() reference, plus a downstream exposure and governance metadata.
codeExamples.code:
version: 2

models:
  - name: fct_orders
    description: "One row per completed order. Grain: order_id. Built from stg_orders joined to customers."
    access: public          # may be ref()'d by other groups
    config:
      tags: ['finance', 'core']
      persist_docs:
        relation: true       # push table comment to warehouse
        columns: true        # push column comments to warehouse
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: "Primary key of the order."
        data_tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: order_status
        description: "{{ doc('order_status') }}"   # reuse a doc block
      - name: amount_usd
        description: "Order total in USD, net of discounts."
        meta:
          contains_pii: false

exposures:
  - name: revenue_dashboard
    type: dashboard
    maturity: high
    url: https://bi.internal/revenue
    description: "Executive revenue dashboard refreshed daily."
    depends_on:
      - ref('fct_orders')
    owner:
      name: Analytics Team
      email: analytics@example.com
codeExamples.breakdown: The model gets a top-level description and access: public so it is a governed interface. persist_docs pushes the relation and column comments into the warehouse. Each column has a description; order_status pulls its text from a shared doc block via doc(). The exposure declares that revenue_dashboard depends_on fct_orders, so it appears downstream in the lineage graph - a change to fct_orders now visibly threatens the dashboard.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: After `dbt run` + `dbt docs generate`, the fct_orders page shows the description, column types (from catalog.json), the resolved order_status text, and a lineage graph with revenue_dashboard as a downstream node. Warehouse table/column comments are populated.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Referencing a doc('order_status') block that does not exist fails docs generate. Forgetting persist_docs means warehouse comments stay empty. Setting access: public without defining a group is fine, but private/protected require the model to belong to a group.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Enforce description coverage in CI; use tags (e.g., 'pii', 'finance') consistently so you can select and audit by tag; keep grain and primary key in every model description for fast onboarding.

codeExamples.title: Doc block in Markdown: reusable {% docs %} ... {% enddocs %}
codeExamples.overview: A .md file defining a reusable, Markdown-formatted documentation block referenced from YAML via doc().
codeExamples.breakdown: Each block is named ({% docs order_status %}) and holds Markdown - here a table and a link. Any YAML description can pull it in with {{ doc('order_status') }}, so the same explanation renders identically on every model/column that uses it. A second pii_notice block shows how to standardize governance language. dbt resolves these blocks at compile time and embeds the text into manifest.json, so the docs site renders formatted output.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: On the docs site, columns whose description is {{ doc('order_status') }} render the formatted table and hyperlink; updating the block once updates every referencing column.
codeExamples.commonIssues: The file must have a .md extension and live in a configured docs path; the block name must be unique across the project. Referencing an undefined block name errors out. Markdown that is valid in a wiki may render slightly differently in the dbt docs site.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep a docs/ directory of shared blocks for enums, PII notices, and common metrics; name blocks by concept (order_status) not by model so they are reusable; use tables and links for high-value context.

codeExamples.title: CLI: generating, serving, and using lineage for impact analysis
codeExamples.overview: Building models, generating docs, serving the site, and using graph selection to find everything downstream of a model.
codeExamples.code:
# 1. Build the models so the catalog can read real column types/stats
dbt build            # runs models + tests (creates relations in the warehouse)

# 2. Compile the project and query the warehouse -> manifest.json + catalog.json
dbt docs generate

# 3. Launch the local documentation website (default http://localhost:8080)
dbt docs serve --port 8080

# 3b. Or produce a single self-contained HTML file to host/share
dbt docs generate --static   # writes target/static_index.html

# 4. Impact analysis WITHOUT the UI: list everything downstream of stg_orders
dbt ls --select stg_orders+          # the model and all its descendants
dbt ls --select +fct_orders          # fct_orders and all its ancestors
dbt ls --select tag:pii              # every resource tagged 'pii'

# 5. CI: build only what changed and its downstream, using a prod manifest
dbt build --select state:modified+ --state ./prod-artifacts
codeExamples.breakdown: dbt build creates the relations so catalog.json can capture real types/stats. dbt docs generate compiles the project (manifest.json) and queries the information schema (catalog.json). dbt docs serve renders the interactive site; --static bakes it into one HTML file. The dbt ls selectors show lineage on the command line: model+ is descendants (downstream impact), +model is ancestors (upstream sources), and state:modified+ (comparing against a stored --state manifest) rebuilds only changed models and their downstream - the backbone of Slim CI.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: docs generate prints something like 'Building catalog\nCatalog written to target/catalog.json'. dbt ls --select stg_orders+ prints the fully-qualified names of stg_orders, int_orders_joined, fct_orders (and the revenue_dashboard exposure). serve prints 'Serving docs at http://localhost:8080'.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Running docs generate without first building leaves catalog gaps (missing types/stats). Forgetting --state (or pointing it at a stale manifest) makes state:modified+ select the wrong set. The + is direction-sensitive: model+ (downstream) vs +model (upstream) is a frequent mix-up.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Automate dbt docs generate in CI and publish the artifacts so viewers never run it locally; use --static for simple hosting; cache the previous production manifest for state selection to slash CI compute.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A jaffle-shop analytics team must onboard new analysts quickly, safely refactor a widely-used staging model, and prove to auditors where PII flows - all without maintaining a hand-drawn diagram or an out-of-date wiki.
endToEndExample.inputData: A layered dbt project: sources (raw.jaffle.orders, raw.jaffle.customers), staging models (stg_orders, stg_customers), an intermediate model (int_orders_enriched), and a mart (fct_orders), plus a schema.yml with descriptions, shared doc blocks, tags, and an exposure for the revenue dashboard.
endToEndExample.architecture: source() declares raw inputs; ref() links staging -> intermediate -> marts, forming the DAG; descriptions live in schema.yml and reusable {% docs %} blocks; persist_docs mirrors descriptions to the warehouse; an exposure represents the downstream dashboard; `dbt build` then `dbt docs generate` produce manifest.json + catalog.json; `dbt docs generate --static` is published by CI for viewers.
processingSteps: 1. Model authoring: engineers write stg_orders (FROM {{ source('jaffle','orders') }}), int_orders_enriched (FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }} joined to stg_customers), and fct_orders (FROM {{ ref('int_orders_enriched') }}), so every dependency is declared via source()/ref().

2. Documentation: schema.yml gets model and column descriptions; the order_status enum and a pii_notice go into shared doc blocks; sensitive columns are tagged 'pii'; an exposure declares revenue_dashboard depends_on ref('fct_orders').

3. Build + generate: CI runs `dbt build` (creating relations and running tests) then `dbt docs generate`, compiling the project into manifest.json (graph + descriptions) and querying the information schema for catalog.json (column types/stats); persist_docs writes warehouse comments.

4. Impact analysis for the refactor: before changing stg_orders, an engineer runs `dbt ls --select stg_orders+` and opens the docs lineage graph, seeing int_orders_enriched, fct_orders, and the revenue_dashboard exposure all downstream - so the blast radius is known before any change ships.

5. Publish + audit: CI runs `dbt docs generate --static` and hosts the single HTML file for analysts; auditors filter by tag:pii and follow lineage from the tagged source columns all the way to fct_orders and the dashboard exposure to prove data flow.
endToEndExample.output: An always-current documentation website with per-model/column descriptions, warehouse-populated comments, an interactive lineage DAG spanning sources -> staging -> intermediate -> marts -> dashboard exposure, and machine-readable manifest.json/catalog.json artifacts.
endToEndExample.monitoring: CI checks documentation coverage (models/columns with descriptions) and fails the build below a threshold; source freshness is monitored; the manifest is diffed against production for state:modified+ selection so only affected models rebuild.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: docs generate fails fast on missing doc() blocks or dependency cycles; catalog gaps signal unbuilt models; the exposure surfaces that a stg_orders change threatens the revenue dashboard, prompting coordination before deploy.
endToEndExample.finalResult: New analysts self-serve via the docs site, refactors are de-risked by one-click impact analysis, PII flow is provable via tags + lineage, and none of it depends on manually maintained diagrams - the graph is a byproduct of the ref()/source() code the team already writes.

industryUseCases.company: Fintech data platform (regulated, e.g. a lending or payments company)
industryUseCases.problem: Auditors require proof of where PII and financial data originate and flow, and any schema change must be assessed for downstream regulatory-report impact.
industryUseCases.solution: Tag PII columns and sources, use exposures for regulatory dashboards, and rely on the dbt lineage DAG plus tag:pii selection to trace data end to end; persist_docs surfaces the same classifications in the warehouse.
industryUseCases.benefits: Provable, always-current data lineage for audits; safe schema changes via impact analysis; reduced manual documentation effort and compliance risk.

industryUseCases.company: Multi-team analytics org (e.g. a large marketplace with many domain teams)
industryUseCases.problem: Hundreds of models across teams lead to accidental cross-team dependencies on internal, unstable models and constant 'what does this column mean?' questions.
industryUseCases.solution: Adopt groups with access modifiers (public/private/protected) so each team exposes only vetted public models, plus rich schema.yml descriptions and shared doc blocks published as a docs site.
industryUseCases.benefits: Clear ownership and stable public interfaces, fewer breaking cross-team changes, and dramatically faster onboarding via self-serve documentation.

industryUseCases.company: Data consultancy / agency onboarding new client projects
industryUseCases.problem: Consultants must understand an unfamiliar warehouse quickly and hand clients a maintainable, self-documenting project.
industryUseCases.solution: Generate `dbt docs --static` for each project so the client gets a portable, browsable model catalog and lineage graph, with descriptions and doc blocks captured in the repo.
industryUseCases.benefits: Faster ramp-up on new codebases, a professional deliverable clients can navigate without dbt installed, and documentation that stays in sync because it lives with the code.

productionDeepDive.scalability: In large projects the manifest is the scaling backbone: partial parsing keeps re-parse times low, groups/access modifiers keep the mental model and interface surface manageable across teams, and state:modified+ selection means CI and prod runs scale with the change set, not the total number of models. Generate docs centrally in CI rather than per-developer.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: dbt rejects dependency cycles and missing doc()/ref() targets at parse time, catching structural errors before execution. Exposures make downstream (dashboard/app) dependencies explicit so a breaking model change is visible up front; keeping ref()/source() usage strict guarantees the executed graph and the documented graph are identical.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: The docs site is static (files rendered from manifest.json/catalog.json), so hosting is trivially highly available - serve the generated artifacts (or --static HTML) from object storage or a CDN with no live database dependency for viewers.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Because documentation and lineage are fully derived from version-controlled code, they are reproducible: regenerating from the repo recreates the manifest and docs exactly. Store production manifests (for state comparison) durably so CI can recover its baseline.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Use partial parsing (default) to speed iterative runs; avoid generating the catalog against enormous wide schemas more often than needed since it issues information-schema queries; publish CI-generated artifacts so end users load a static site instead of recompiling locally.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: state:modified+ rebuilds only changed models and their descendants, cutting warehouse compute in CI and prod; persist_docs lets warehouse consumers read descriptions from table/column comments instead of ad-hoc discovery queries; catalog generation can be scoped to control its metadata-query cost.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Classify sensitive columns with tags (e.g. 'pii') and meta, then use lineage for data-flow audits; enforce access modifiers so teams cannot depend on another team's private models; remember a public docs site exposes schema, column names, and descriptions, so host it behind appropriate access controls if that is sensitive.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track documentation coverage (percent of models/columns documented), enforce it in CI (e.g. dbt-checkpoint), monitor source freshness, and watch for catalog gaps that indicate unbuilt models; treat the manifest as the observability contract other tools consume.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Pair descriptions with data_tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) in the same schema.yml so documentation and validation live together; contracts plus access:public turn a model into an enforced, documented interface.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Fail CI on missing descriptions, undefined doc blocks, dependency cycles, or contract violations; alert when source freshness lapses or when an exposure's upstream model is modified, so downstream dashboard owners are notified before deploy.

recommendedPractices: **Always use ref() and source()** for every dependency - never hard-code a warehouse table name - so lineage and build order are automatic and accurate.
**Document grain and primary key in every model description**, and give every column a meaningful description; enforce coverage in CI.
**Factor shared/long descriptions into {% docs %} blocks** referenced with doc() so common concepts (enums, PII notices, metrics) are written once and reused.
**Generate docs in CI/CD and publish the artifacts** (or --static HTML) so the site and manifest stay current for everyone without manual local runs.
engineeringStandards: Enforce ref()/source() usage and description coverage with linters/tools (dbt-checkpoint, SQLFluff) in CI to prevent lineage bypass and undocumented models.
Use groups and access modifiers (public/private/protected) in multi-team projects to define ownership and stable public interfaces.
Store the production manifest and use state:modified+ selection so CI rebuilds only what changed and its downstream.
designRecommendations: Follow the layered staging -> intermediate -> marts structure so the lineage graph reads clearly and dependencies flow one direction.
Model exposures for every downstream consumer (dashboards, apps, ML) so impact analysis reaches beyond the warehouse.
Set persist_docs when consumers query the warehouse directly, keeping a single source of truth for descriptions.
namingConventions: Prefix models by layer (stg_, int_, fct_/dim_) so lineage and folders are self-explanatory.
Name doc blocks by concept (order_status, pii_notice) rather than by model, so they are reusable across resources.
Use consistent, controlled tags (e.g. 'pii', 'finance', 'core') so tag-based selection and audits are reliable.
documentationStandards: Every model description states its grain, primary key, and purpose; every column description explains meaning and units.
Use doc() blocks with Markdown tables/links for enums and shared context; keep them in a dedicated docs/ folder.
Document access level and ownership (via access + groups/exposure owner) so consumers know stability and who to contact.
testingStrategies: Co-locate data_tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) with descriptions in schema.yml so validation and documentation ship together.
Add a CI check that fails on undefined doc() references and dependency cycles before merge.
Verify catalog completeness by building models before docs generate, and gate merges on documentation-coverage thresholds.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hard-coding table names in FROM clauses instead of using ref()/source().
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Copying legacy SQL, or a quick fix where the author knows the exact schema.table name and skips the Jinja function.
commonMistakes.impact: The model is invisible to the lineage graph and build ordering - dbt may build it in the wrong order and the docs lineage is silently incomplete, defeating impact analysis.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always reference other models with {{ ref('model') }} and raw tables with {{ source('src','tbl') }}; add a linter check to reject raw table references in models.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running `dbt docs generate` expecting a complete catalog without building the models first.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming docs generate runs/refreshes the models, or generating docs in an environment where relations were never created.
commonMistakes.impact: catalog.json is missing column types and stats for unbuilt relations, so the docs site shows models without column type information and looks broken.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Run `dbt build` (or dbt run) first so the relations exist, then `dbt docs generate`; in CI, order the steps accordingly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Referencing a doc() block that does not exist, or duplicating block names.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Typos in the block name, renaming/removing a .md block without updating YAML, or defining two blocks with the same name in different files.
commonMistakes.impact: docs generate (and compilation) fails, blocking the pipeline; duplicate names cause ambiguous references and parse errors.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Keep doc blocks in a dedicated folder with unique, concept-based names; add a CI step that compiles the project so missing/duplicate references fail fast in review.

comparisonSection.explanation: Inline descriptions are fastest for one-off, short text local to a single model/column. Doc blocks let you write rich Markdown (tables, links) once and reference it from many resources with {{ doc('name') }}, so shared concepts like enums or PII notices stay consistent and update everywhere at once. Use inline for simple unique text; use doc blocks for anything shared, long, or formatted.

dbt docs serve spins up a local server reading target/manifest.json and catalog.json - ideal for interactive local exploration during development. --static bakes everything into one self-contained static_index.html that can be hosted on object storage/CDN or emailed, requiring no dbt install for viewers; it is the right choice for sharing with stakeholders or CI-published documentation, at the cost of being a point-in-time snapshot that must be regenerated to stay current.

beginnerQuestions.question: How does dbt build the lineage graph, and do you have to maintain it manually?
beginnerQuestions.answer: dbt builds the lineage graph automatically by statically parsing the ref() and source() functions in your SQL. Each ref('model') creates an edge to another dbt model and each source('name','table') an edge from a raw table, forming a directed acyclic graph. You never maintain it manually - as long as you use ref()/source(), the graph is always accurate.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The key point is that lineage is derived from the same dependency calls dbt uses for build order, so it cannot drift from reality. Mention that hard-coding table names breaks this.

beginnerQuestions.question: What do `dbt docs generate` and `dbt docs serve` do?
beginnerQuestions.answer: `dbt docs generate` compiles the project and writes two artifacts: manifest.json (nodes, config, descriptions, and dependency edges) and catalog.json (column types and stats queried from the warehouse information schema). `dbt docs serve` starts a local web server that renders those artifacts as a documentation website with per-model pages and an interactive lineage graph.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Clarify that docs generate does not run your models - it compiles them and queries the information schema for already-built relations, which is why you build first for a complete catalog.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between manifest.json and catalog.json?
intermediateQuestions.answer: manifest.json is the code-derived artifact: every node with its compiled SQL, config, descriptions (doc blocks resolved), tags, and depends_on edges - effectively the graph plus metadata. catalog.json is the warehouse-derived artifact: per-relation column names, data types, and statistics gathered by querying the information schema. manifest reflects the code; catalog reflects the live database.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize manifest.json's second life: it powers state comparison (state:modified+) and is consumed by external tooling, not just the docs site.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do doc blocks work and when would you use them over inline descriptions?
intermediateQuestions.answer: You define a named block with {% docs block_name %}...Markdown...{% enddocs %} in a .md file and reference it in any YAML description as "{{ doc('block_name') }}". dbt resolves it at compile time. Use doc blocks for long, Markdown-rich, or shared descriptions (enums, PII notices, metric definitions) so you write once and reuse everywhere; use inline text for short, unique descriptions.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Call out that a missing or duplicated block name fails compilation - a common CI catch.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you perform impact analysis before refactoring a heavily-used staging model?
advancedQuestions.answer: Use the lineage graph and graph selection. On the CLI, `dbt ls --select stg_orders+` lists the model and all its descendants; the docs site highlights the same downstream nodes including any exposures. That reveals every model and dashboard that would be affected. I'd also check exposures to see BI/app dependencies and coordinate with owners before shipping.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Show you know the + direction: model+ is downstream (descendants/impact), +model is upstream (ancestors/sources). Mention exposures extend impact analysis beyond the warehouse.

advancedQuestions.question: How do exposures, groups, and access modifiers extend documentation and governance?
advancedQuestions.answer: Exposures are YAML nodes representing downstream consumers (dashboards, apps, ML) that depend_on models, so lineage reaches past the warehouse and impact analysis includes BI. Groups bundle models under an owner, and access modifiers (public/private/protected) control whether a model can be ref()'d from outside its group - turning models into governed interfaces. Together they add ownership, safe public contracts, and end-to-end lineage.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tie access to multi-team scaling: private/protected prevent teams from coupling to another team's internal, unstable models.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your docs site renders models but every column shows no data type, and stakeholders think the docs are broken. Analysts also complain the site is a week out of date. What is happening and how do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Missing column types point to an incomplete catalog.json - the models were not built before docs generate, so the information-schema query found nothing. The stale site means docs are generated manually/locally rather than in CI, so they reflect an old snapshot. Both are process fixes: build before generate, and automate generation in CI.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Run `dbt build` (or dbt run) before `dbt docs generate` so relations exist and catalog.json can capture column types/stats. Then move doc generation into CI/CD - run build, then docs generate (or --static), and publish the artifacts to the hosted site on every merge - so the documentation is always current for viewers and nobody depends on a local run.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a documentation and lineage system for a 500-model dbt project shared by five domain teams, with regulatory PII-tracing requirements and fast CI.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Enforce ref()/source() everywhere so lineage is automatic and accurate. Organize models into per-team groups with access modifiers so each team exposes only vetted public models. Document grain/PK/columns in schema.yml, use shared doc blocks for enums and a standard pii_notice, and tag PII columns. Model exposures for every dashboard/app. In CI: dbt build (or state:modified+), then dbt docs generate --static, publish to a CDN; enforce description coverage and reject undefined doc blocks/cycles.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Groups/access add upfront design overhead but prevent cross-team breakage; a static published site is a snapshot so it must be regenerated per merge; catalog generation adds information-schema query cost on wide schemas. persist_docs duplicates descriptions into the warehouse but gives warehouse consumers a single source of truth.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Use partial parsing and state:modified+ so CI compute scales with the change set, not model count; generate docs centrally in CI rather than per-developer; host artifacts on object storage/CDN for HA; classify PII via tags/meta and rely on lineage for audit traces so compliance scales without manual diagrams.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: dbt auto-derives a lineage DAG from ref()/source() calls and pairs it with repo-based descriptions and doc blocks; `dbt docs generate` writes manifest.json (graph) and catalog.json (warehouse types) that a served site renders with an interactive lineage graph.
keyConcepts: ref() and source() are the only source of the lineage DAG and build order - never hard-code table names.
descriptions live in schema.yml (model + column); reuse long/shared text via {% docs %} blocks referenced with {{ doc('name') }}.
docs generate -> manifest.json (nodes, edges, descriptions) + catalog.json (column types/stats from the information schema); build first for a complete catalog.
docs serve renders the interactive site; --static bakes one HTML file; model+ is downstream impact, +model is upstream.
exposures extend lineage to dashboards/apps; groups + access (public/private/protected), meta, tags, and persist_docs add governance.
interviewPoints: Lineage is auto-derived from ref()/source() and cannot drift from the executed graph.
manifest.json = code/graph + descriptions; catalog.json = warehouse column types/stats; build before generate.
doc() blocks give reusable Markdown documentation; missing/duplicate names fail compilation.
model+ (downstream/impact) vs +model (upstream/sources); exposures reach beyond the warehouse.
groups + access modifiers create governed public interfaces; persist_docs mirrors descriptions to the warehouse.
quickNotes: docs generate does NOT run models; it compiles them and queries the information schema for built relations.
Cycles in the DAG are hard errors; the graph must be acyclic.
state:modified+ (with --state pointing at a prior manifest) rebuilds only changed models + downstream - the basis of Slim CI.
Column-level lineage generally needs dbt Cloud/Explorer; node-level lineage is free in open source.
Layer prefixes (stg_/int_/fct_) plus tags make the lineage graph and selection self-explanatory.

keyTakeaways: dbt derives the entire lineage DAG automatically from ref() and source() calls, so the graph is always accurate, requires zero manual upkeep, and is identical to the graph dbt uses to order the build - which is why consistent ref()/source() usage is non-negotiable.

Documentation lives in the repo: write model and column descriptions in schema.yml and factor shared/long prose into reusable {% docs %} blocks referenced with {{ doc('name') }}, so docs ship in the same PR as the code and never rot.

`dbt docs generate` produces manifest.json (nodes, edges, descriptions - also the backbone of state:modified+ CI) and catalog.json (column types/stats from the warehouse information schema), and `dbt docs serve` (or --static) renders them as an interactive site; build your models first for a complete catalog.

Lineage powers impact analysis, debugging, and onboarding: model+ shows downstream descendants (blast radius) and +model shows upstream ancestors, while exposures extend the graph to dashboards and apps so you can see BI breakage before it ships.

Governance features - groups with public/private/protected access, meta and tags, and persist_docs - turn a large multi-team project into a set of documented, owned, auditable interfaces, with descriptions mirrored into the warehouse as a single source of truth.
